metadata.title: Build the Defects First
metadata.note: cli-explainer spine, weekly work-report application, built to the PROOF rubric. INTRO (spoken name) · PROBLEM · FRAMEWORK (the reusable 4-step method, shown as a structure BEFORE any example) · cycle 1 (ASK/CODE/OUTPUT) · cycle 2 (ASK/CODE/OUTPUT) · FALSIFIABILITY · SUMMARY · NEXT STEPS (scaffolded task with good/bad answer) · OUTRO. Voice is Kokoro am_onyx (male) per author request; register stays Pragmatist. Channel @HumanitariansAI, so the @NikBearBrown outro lock is deliberately overridden. Every on-screen number is verified against commit 9ef4e7f and a live run of the script — see SOURCES.md and FACTCHECK.md.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — open on the Claude UI, ask shown answered. Speaks the author's name.
beats.narration_text: I'm Uday Sonawane, and this is my week on Mycroft. Six steps marked to-do, nothing behind them. I did not start with the code.
beats.new_visual_element: Claude composer, the week's opening ask, answered

shot.show: the Claude composer with the week's opening ask and its three-line answer

props.command: claude "the market-sentiment recipe has six TODO steps and no test data — where do I start?"
props.segment: Uday Sonawane · Build the Defects First
output: start with the corpus, not the checker

beats.role_note: the stakes, stated before the method — kept tight so the FRAMEWORK lands inside the first ~20s
beats.narration_text: The recipe declares six development steps. None had an implementation. The tempting move is to write the validator first. But if nothing in your test data is broken, passing is not evidence.

shot.show: six [TODO: DEV] step rows, all unimplemented, with an empty six-cell ledger bar
shot.visual_intent: Six step rows, each with a hollow status box drawn one at a time; none fills. A six-cell ledger bar draws empty beneath. Spark resolves in terracotta: six declared, zero implemented.

beats.role_note: PROOF rubric — the reusable method shown AS A STRUCTURE, before any example. The axes a viewer can apply to their own suite.
beats.narration_text: So here is the method, and it runs on any pipeline. One: enumerate the classes of wrong your data can be. Two: plant one instance of each, and record exactly where it sits. Three: name the check that must catch it. Four: freeze every timestamp, so two runs stay comparable. Do those four, and your validators become gradeable instead of merely runnable.
beats.new_visual_element: the four-step method, as a numbered structure

shot.show: four numbered method cards: ENUMERATE / PLANT / NAME THE CATCHER / FREEZE
shot.visual_intent: Four numbered cards spring into a row, each with a verb and a one-line rule. They stay on screen as the reusable rubric; the closing line lands in terracotta — gradeable, not merely runnable. This is the graphic every later beat is scored against.

beats.role_note: cycle 1 ask — SPARK-LINE LAW: greeting is the spark line
beats.narration_text: That is what I asked for first: the corpus, not the checker. Three clean fixtures, one per stream — Alpha Vantage prices, Finnhub news, Reddit posts — then deliberately broken copies, with every defect written down.

shot.show: the Claude composer carrying the fixture-corpus prompt

props.command: claude "build a frozen sample corpus for this recipe: 3 clean fixtures, one per stream, then defective copies — and catalogue every defect with its locator"

beats.role_note: THE ACTUAL-CODE LAW + PROOF worked example — method step 3 walked through on a real record
beats.narration_text: Here is step three of the method, as it actually sits in the manifest. Defect five records its class, its exact locator, and the step and output field that must surface it. It is a syndicated story: different id, different url, identical headline. An id-only dedupe walks straight past it, and inflates the news denominator.

props.title: data/raw/.../sample/fixture-manifest.json

beats.role_note: cycle 1 output — MOVING, never a still. Method steps 1 and 4 shown at full scale.
beats.narration_text: Run step one of the method across the set and you get eighteen defects in seven classes. Duplicates, missing required fields, malformed rows, stale timestamps, type violations, an envelope count mismatch, and one file that will not parse at all. Every timestamp is pinned to a frozen value, never to now. That is step four.
beats.new_visual_element: the defect catalogue resolving into seven classes

shot.show: 18 numbered defect chips grouped into 7 labelled class rows
shot.visual_intent: Seven class labels land together, then D01 through D18 resolve into them as chips — a histogram by construction. Total line, then the frozen_at pin in terracotta.

beats.role_note: THE REVISION LAW — cycle 2 begins; check the output, change the ask
beats.narration_text: With something to catch, the checker becomes gradeable. So the second ask is step one of the recipe itself: verify provenance, before anything ingests or scores a row.

shot.show: the Claude composer carrying the step-1 prompt

props.command: claude "now write step 1 against that corpus: verify every declared source exists, hashes, and parses — and make a missing required source a hard stop"
output: exit 1 on a missing required source

beats.role_note: THE ACTUAL-CODE LAW — real source, verify-provenance.py, the digest basis
beats.narration_text: The detail that matters is what the digest is computed over. Path, existence, size, hash, parse result, and deliberately not the timestamps. Two runs over unchanged files produce the same digest, so a reviewer can compare them, and any byte change anywhere shows up as a different number.

props.title: scripts/tools/...-verify-provenance.py
props.code:
# Deterministic digest over the findings only - timestamps are
# deliberately excluded so two runs over unchanged files produce
# the same digest and a reviewer can compare them.
digest_basis = [
    {k: f[k] for k in ('path', 'exists', 'size_bytes',
                       'sha256', 'parsed_ok', 'verdict')}
    for f in findings
]
findings_digest = hashlib.sha256(
    json.dumps(digest_basis, sort_keys=True, default=str).encode('utf-8')
).hexdigest()

beats.role_note: cycle 2 output — the better output, MOVING. Real run, real verdicts.
beats.narration_text: Fourteen declared sources, checked for existence, size, hash and parseability. Eight parse clean. Three are present but not parse-checked, because they are markdown, not data. One is unparseable, exactly as the manifest says it should be. Two are absent, and neither is required yet. A missing required source exits nonzero: a hard stop, not a warning.
beats.new_visual_element: 14 source rows resolving to four verdicts

shot.show: 14 source-path rows resolving into OK / present / expected-unparseable / missing chips
shot.visual_intent: Two columns of seven paths land first, then each row resolves into a bordered verdict chip. A proportional bar tallies 8 / 3 / 1 / 2. The exit-code rule lands last in terracotta.

beats.role_note: PROOF rubric — the case that BREAKS the framework, taken from the manifest's own not_covered section
beats.narration_text: Now the case that breaks the method. A row can be well formed, fresh, unique, and complete on every required field, and still belong to the wrong company. Step one cannot enumerate that class, because it is not a shape at all. The manifest says so in writing, in a not-covered section, because that is the class that reached a finished brief.
beats.new_visual_element: a clean row that passes every shape check and is still wrong

shot.show: one record passing four shape checks, side by side with the verdict that it is the wrong entity
shot.visual_intent: A record card holds at top. Four shape checks tick in at left. At right, the terracotta verdict box: but it is the wrong company. Both halves stay on screen together and are held, so the comparison is visible at the moment it is asserted.

beats.role_note: the ledger — what shipped and what did not, with the source named on screen
beats.narration_text: So, the week. Ten files, about twelve hundred lines, one of six steps closed. The rest is open, and openly so. The run envelope does not exist, so gate two cannot clear, and the recipe's six to-do markers still stand.
beats.new_visual_element: the week's ledger — shipped versus still open

shot.show: two-column ledger: shipped this week versus still open, with the commit named
shot.visual_intent: Left column fills: 10 files, 1198 lines, step 1 of 6, 18/18 locators. Right column stays terracotta and unfinished: 5 steps, run-envelope absent, gate 2 blocked, 6 TODO markers. Kicker names the commit.

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW + PROOF active-task rule — a runnable scaffold, read aloud, with what a good and a bad answer look like
beats.narration_text: Your turn: run the method on your own suite. Paste this prompt. List every check in my validator, and for each one, name the defect in my fixtures that would make it fail. A good answer names a fixture and a line for every check. A bad answer tells you the tests pass. If a check has no matching defect, it is not passing. It has nothing to catch.
beats.new_visual_element: Claude composer, the handoff prompt typed in

shot.show: the Claude composer with the viewer's suggested prompt and the good/bad test

props.command: claude "list every check in my validator. For each, name the defect in my fixtures that would make it fail, with file and line. Flag every check nothing in the corpus can trip."
output: GOOD: a fixture + line for every check
no matching defect = nothing to catch
